original_question: Find additional settings in extremal set theory or related areas where a compression proof can be rescued by using a collection of alternative compression operators, even though no single operator is guaranteed to decrease the relevant boundary or objective in every instance.
target_in_paper: Section 10, Question 10.2 ('Pinto’s Alternative Compressions: a technique in search of more applications').
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the core of the paper’s open problem: the search for further applications of Pinto’s 'alternative compressions' idea, where a compression proof can still succeed even though no single compression is monotone for the target quantity in every case.
missing_details: The ambient setting motivating the question is the Boolean lattice / hypercube Q_n = P([n]), not an arbitrary compression framework.
The motivating application is Theorem 10.1: for disjoint A,B ⊆ Q_n with A a down-set, B an up-set, and |A| = |B| = 2^k, there are at least 2^k(n-k) edge-disjoint upwards-directed paths from A to B.

The two prototype operators should be named and defined: for a fixed coordinate i, C_i removes every set in F that contains i but whose i-deletion is not already in F, while D_i adds every set not containing i whose i-extension already lies in F.
The quantity that fails to be monotone in the prototype application is specifically the upwards directed edge boundary of a family, not just an unspecified 'boundary or objective'.

The paper’s key non-simultaneous-badness principle should be stated explicitly: although C_i and D_i may each increase the directed boundary on some examples, they cannot both be bad for the same family in the needed way.

The compression choice is adaptive: at each step one chooses whichever operator from the available collection behaves well for the current family; the proof does not use a single fixed operator throughout.
The official question asks only for 'some more applications' of this proof twist, not for a classification theorem or a general abstract theory of all such phenomena.

To make the question fully stand-alone, one should mention that the method is presented as a rescue of a natural compression approach that initially 'looks doomed to fail' in Pinto’s Boolean-cube argument.
refined_question: Find further applications of Pinto’s alternative-compressions method in the Boolean-lattice/compression style of extremal set theory: for families F ⊆ Q_n = P([n]), fix a coordinate i and consider the two i-direction operations that either delete every set S in F containing i whose lower shadow S with i removed is absent from F, or add every set S not containing i for which S with i added already lies in F. In Pinto’s prototype application, neither operation by itself is guaranteed to decrease the upwards directed edge boundary of a family, but the two operations cannot both fail simultaneously, so one can choose adaptively at each step and still complete a compression proof. Identify other problems where this same non-simultaneous-badness principle rescues an otherwise failing compression argument.
equivalent_formulation: Find some more applications where this twist on the compression method can be used to rescue a compression proof; that is, arguments in which any single compression operator is not guaranteed to behave well in all situations, but where this bad behaviour cannot occur simultaneously for a larger collection of compressions.
justification: The draft is aimed directly at Section 10, especially Question 10.2. The section introduces Pinto’s method as 'a technique in search of more applications', gives Theorem 10.1 as the motivating success case, then explains the two candidate i-direction compressions C_i and D_i on families in Q_n and why neither alone gives a monotone compression proof for the upwards directed edge boundary. The official open problem is precisely to find more applications of this rescue mechanism. Your draft already captures that idea well, but it leaves implicit the Boolean-cube setting, the actual operators, the prototype objective function, and the adaptive/non-simultaneous-badness feature that makes the method work.
